zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The supplied page subset was consulted after independent scan reading for lexical and coverage comparison. Corrections and English comments are reviewer-authored; this copy's printed forms are determined from its scan.

lines.note: Norisonji introduces riding badly or contrary to proper practice. The zuru and ita principal parts belong to norisonzuru; the Portuguese qualification continues on the next row.

runs.text: a regra, & ordem do caualgar. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Completes the riding sense as violating its rules and order. Item introduces an additional, less exact use rather than a new headword.

runs.text: minùs propriè, Caualgando danar, ou tratar

lines.note: Latin minùs propriè qualifies the following sense as less proper: damaging or mistreating something while riding. The mark over u is a grave, like that over the final e, not a nasal-abbreviation tilde.
The mistreated object is the horse. Fune wo norisonzuru then applies the same verb to navigating a boat badly; Na- begins the Portuguese verb continued below.

runs.text: uegar mal, ou por a parte que não deuera.

lines.note: Completes Na-uegar and explains going by an improper route. The boat example extends the riding verb to navigation, not to harming the horse again.
Norisute, norisutsuru, norisuteta denotes dismounting and leaving the horse behind. The lar- belongs to largar on the following physical line.

After completing largar o caualo, fune wo norisutsuru describes abandoning a boat on disembarking. The second pass and enlargement retain the supplied hyphen after Deſ: a weak broken mark is visible to the right of ſ, so the first-pass omission was withdrawn.

runs.text: embarcandoſe botar a embarcação por hi.

lines.note: Completes Deſembarcandoſe: after getting out, leave the vessel lying about. Por hi is retained as printed, not modernized to a present-day expression.
Noritsuke first means being accustomed to riding or boarding. Acustumado is the visible historical Portuguese spelling; the nasal abbreviation in ẽ- begins embarcar across the break.
Completes embarcar and introduces fune or uma as the vehicle ridden. The scan reads Fune, boat, rather than the OCR's Fone; l gives the alternative before the next line.
Uma ni noritsukuru completes the habitual-riding example. A new construction, fune wo noritsukuru, then introduces bringing a vessel up to a destination or to others.

runs.text: Chegar com a Fune a algum porto, ou

lines.note: Completes noritsukuru. The Portuguese says to arrive with the boat at a port; Japanese Fune is embedded in that explanation and is not an additional headword.

runs.text: ſurgidouro, ou fazer ir a embarcação pegada,

lines.note: Surgidouro supplies an anchorage as an alternative destination. The next sense has the vessel travel closely alongside or behind others, continued on the following row.

runs.text: ou junto com as que vão diante. ¶

lines.note: The boats ahead complete the close-following sense. Vmauo starts the corresponding horse example, with the object particle attached as printed.

runs.text: Ir logo de tras, ou no alcã-

lines.note: Uma wo noritsukuru is riding immediately behind or close upon others. The printed alcã- abbreviates the nasal in alcance; its terminal division is visible.

runs.text: ce dos que vão diante a caualo. ¶

lines.note: Completes alcance and specifies people riding in front. Noritçu- begins the imperative example inviting someone to draw nearer, continued below.
Noritsukete gozare asks the listener to come closer while riding. The Portuguese is a directive to approach, with the reference point supplied on the next row.

runs.text: dos caualos ou Norimonos, que vão diante.

lines.note: The listener is to approach the horses or norimono conveyances ahead. Norimonos occurs within the Portuguese explanation, with its printed plural ending retained.
Noritsure means travelling in company while riding or embarked. The initial o has no secure vowel-length mark: the apparent OCR caron in Nǒritçure is not supported by the letter area.
Completes embarcandoſe and states the shared sense of going in company. This is a physical continuation of noritsure, not a separate entry.
Noritodome denotes stopping or holding back the horse being ridden. The alternative object, the vessel, continues below.
The vessel completes the pair of objects that may be stopped. This short row belongs entirely to noritodome.

The verb denotes taking a fortress by mounting or climbing into it. The first printed form is retained as Noritoru despite the expected principal-part pattern; the faint line-end point after ſubin is also retained rather than regularized to a hyphen.

runs.text: do a ella por manha, ou enganos eſcõdidamẽte.

lines.note: Completes subindo: entering the fortress secretly by cunning or deception. The compressed nasal spellings in eſcõdidamẽte are preserved, not expanded in the transcription.
Noriwatari is glossed simply as navigating or travelling by water. The printed u and atta are abbreviated principal parts, not independent Japanese words.
Noriwatashi means crossing by boat or while riding. The visible v before ataxi restores the syllable wa omitted by OCR; aita is the historical s-verb past form and is not modernized to ashita.
Kawa wo noriwatasu illustrates crossing a river. The Portuguese reads caualo, with a damaged v, rather than canalo; the means of crossing is completed below.

runs.text: a ribeira a caualo, ou na embarcação.

lines.note: Completes the river-crossing translation: on horseback or in a vessel. Ribeira here supplies the watercourse crossed, not a separate destination on its bank.
Noriukabe denotes setting a boat afloat. Fune is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese causative explanation, while nadar describes floating rather than a person swimming.

runs.text: ou polla em muita agoa de maneira que nade.

lines.note: The explanation restates launching as putting the boat into sufficient water to float. Polla and agoa retain the historical Portuguese forms visible in the scan.
Noriukabi gives the corresponding intransitive sense: the vessel floats. The caron in ǒda is visible; the following clause specifies an occupied vessel.
Specifies that people are aboard the floating vessel. The grave in està is preserved as printed, independently of modern Portuguese accentuation.

runs.text: Caualo de ſella. Mas mais propria-

lines.note: Noriuma is a saddle horse, more precisely the horse someone rides. The first letter of ſella is long s, not f; the Portuguese saddle sense supports the visible type.

runs.text: mente caualo em que hum caualga.

lines.note: Completes propriamente and narrows the definition to a horse actually ridden by someone. This qualification belongs to noriuma rather than introducing another riding verb.
Noriokure first means being left behind without embarking with the others. The printed vo sequence is retained; the interpretation does not require replacing it with modern spelling.

runs.text: car com os outros. ¶ Item, Ficar detras

lines.note: Completes embarcar with the others, then adds lagging behind as a second sense. The objects of detras appear on the following line.

runs.text: das outras embarcaçoens ou dos que vão diante

lines.note: The lagging traveller falls behind other vessels or people ahead. Embarcaçoens is the visible historical plural and is not standardized.
Specifies that the people ahead are on horseback, completing the two travel settings for noriokure. The short continuation is ordinary body text.
Noriutsuri denotes transferring from one vessel to another. The Portuguese reflexive is Paſſarſe, not OCR Paſſarte; em- begins embarcação across the line break.

runs.text: barcação a outra. ¶ Item, Entrar o diabo

lines.note: Finishes the vessel-transfer sense and introduces possession by a devil as another use of noriutsuru. The person entered is specified below.
Completes the possession gloss and begins the example 'in that person's heart'. The Japanese locative-topic sequence niua is attached to cocoro as printed.

Tenma fajun is the demonic agent of possession; norivtçutta is the past of noriutsuru, with the visible v restored after nori. Xid. is the printed citation label, left unexpanded; Entra- begins the translation.

runs.text: rão os diabos no corpo daquelle homem.

lines.note: Completes Entrarão and translates the example as devils entering that man's body. The Portuguese renders the Japanese heart-expression more broadly as the person's body.
Noriyaburi means damaging or maltreating the vessel one travels in. The past ending utta is retained as the printed principal part.

runs.text: a embarcação os que vam nella.

lines.note: The people aboard are the agents who mistreat the vessel. The printed vam is preserved rather than standardized to vão.
Noroi denotes uttering curses. The two circumflex-marked principal parts are kept; Item introduces another description of the same harmful invocation.

runs.text: Fazer deprecaçoens pera que venha mal, ou

lines.note: The invocation asks that evil should befall someone. Deprecaçoens is retained as the historical Portuguese noun rather than replaced with a modern paraphrase in the transcription.
Death is the final alternative harm sought in the curse. This last line closes the entry and the column; it is not page furniture.
Noroigoto means words of cursing; noroigoto wo yuu illustrates uttering them. The final verb visibly has u with a caron, yǔ, not OCR yô.
The Portuguese translates the preceding example as saying curses. This short indented row closes noroigoto.

runs.text: Fogo queſe aleuanta por ſinal dalgũa cou

lines.note: Noroshi is a signal fire. The visible cou continues as couſa on the next row without a terminal hyphen; the right rule is included in the crop.
Completes couſa and gives noroshi wo aguru, raising a signal fire. The Portuguese eſ- begins este across the physical break.
Completes the translation as raising this fire for a signal. The row is the end of the noroshi entry, not part of the following word for ability.
Noosai denotes arts, learning, or knowledge. The same word is divided as Nô-ſai in the example; both visible circumflexes are retained.

runs.text: Homem que tem artes, ou ha-

lines.note: Noosai aru hito is a person possessing skills or learning. The Portuguese ha- begins habilidades on the next row.
Completes habilidades and adds knowledge to the description. It supplies the abilities of the person in the Japanese example.
Noosoo is a learned or wise Buddhist monk. Both vowels bear circumflexes here; the following similar-looking agricultural entry has a different final mark and short s.

runs.text: O cultiuar, ou criar, & tratar bem a-

lines.note: This noosoo entry concerns cultivation and careful tending, specifically of mulberries. The scan preserves short s and final caron in Nôsǒ, distinct from the preceding monk headword.

Completes amoreiras and explains their use in silk production. The final S. is an upright written-register label, outside the italic Portuguese gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Noosui is paraphrased by yoi mizzu, good water, and directly translated as Boa agoa. The Japanese paraphrase is not an embedded Portuguese term; final S. is the upright register label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Notamai is speech by a high-ranking person. The supplied past form notamaixi and the caron in ǒ belong to the historical honorific verb, not a modernized notamau paradigm.

runs.text: Vſaſe deste verbo nos liuros, & prègaçoẽs.

lines.note: The usage note places the honorific verb in books and preaching. The historical spelling and printed vowel marks in prègaçoẽs are retained rather than regularized.
Notame names an implement for straightening arrows. This row begins its physical description, whose cut and purpose are completed below.

runs.text: meo ao reues pera endereitar frechas, &c.

lines.note: The instrument is cut across its middle and used to straighten arrows. Meo, reues, and frechas are transcribed as printed, not replaced with modern Portuguese forms.
Notamegata denotes the shape of the arrow-straightening implement just described. The following example extends that physical shape into a figurative manner of acting or speaking.
Notamegata ni suru or yuu is explicitly marked figurative by Per met. The two Japanese verbs mean doing and saying; the characterization follows below.

runs.text: Fazer, ou dizer as couſas refolhadamente, &

lines.note: The Portuguese describes doing or saying things with concealment or evasiveness. Refolhadamente is retained as the printed word, linked to the absence of simplicity on the next row.
Without straightforwardness completes the figurative gloss of notamegata. The phrase is not an independent definition of simplicity.
Nootsuu is paraphrased by nayami itamu, suffering and hurting. The Portuguese reads debilita-, with a visible b rather than OCR l, and describes a greatly weakened condition.

runs.text: do, & doente, ou mal dalgũa ferida, inchaço,

lines.note: Completes debilitado and adds illness or distress from a wound or swelling. The phrase elaborates the bodily suffering of the preceding Japanese paraphrase.

Ends the illustrative causes of suffering and adds the upright S. written-register label. Even this brief continuation belongs to the nootsuu entry. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Notori no koma is a horse caught in the wild. The relative clause continues below and distinguishes it from a fully tamed horse.
The wild-caught horse is not yet well tamed. The scan includes t in domeſticado, omitted by OCR; the negative and grave-marked està are retained.
Nowaki is a strong wind. The example begins with hashitanoo, harshly or violently, divided in the print as faxita-nǒ; the Portuguese below makes the force of the wind explicit.

runs.text: nǒ fuite, côyô mina fuqi chiraſu.

lines.note: Completes faxitanǒ and says the wind blows all the autumn foliage about. The two circumflexes in côyô are visible; fuqi chiraſu retains its printed space.

runs.text: to do Outono ventando rijo eſpalha, & derru-

lines.note: Completes vento: the autumn wind blows hard, scatters, and knocks down the leaves. Derru- continues as derruba on the next row.

runs.text: ba as folhas vermelhas, & velhas das aruores.

lines.note: The objects scattered are the trees' red and old leaves. This completes the Portuguese interpretation of kooyoo in the example without altering the Japanese spelling.
Nose means making someone embark or ride. The abbreviated ſuru is the headword's historical principal-part ending, not a separate instruction to do something.

runs.text: Por algũa couſa a os õ-

lines.note: Kata ni nosuru means placing something on the shoulders. The damaged Japanese letters support Catani; the Portuguese õ- begins ombros, with its nasal abbreviation preserved.
Completes ombros, then gives ni wo nosuru, loading baggage. The translation contrasts putting goods aboard with placing them on a pack animal below.
Completes the loading example by placing the baggage on a beast of burden. Pollo retains the printed historical object-pronoun construction.

runs.text: Hum instrumento de metal como eſquẽ-

lines.note: Noshi names a metal pressing implement, compared with a warmer. The capital is N, not OCR X, and instrumento is a single printed word; the supplied st allograph is retained because the ligature does not securely decide s versus ſ.

runs.text: tador, em que metem fogo peratirar as dobras

lines.note: Completes esquentador: fire is put inside the implement to remove creases. The close peratirar spacing is retained rather than silently regularized.
The implement smooths clothing and allows it to be folded neatly. This closes the noun entry before the corresponding verb begins.
Noshi, nosu, noita is the verb for extending or removing creases. The past ending oita is historical s-verb morphology and is not replaced by modern oshita.
The first sense uses the preceding implement. Se wo nosu then means straightening the back; Xe is ordinary Jesuit spelling for se, not an erroneous consonant.
Completes Endereitarſe: a bent person straightens up. The visible it restores dereitarſe rather than OCR dereuarſe; Coxiuo begins the parallel waist or lower-back example.
Koshi wo nosu has the same straightening sense. Shiwa wo nosu then concerns removing folds or wrinkles, with the affected material specified below.

runs.text: do veſtido, ou estender as rugas da carne, &c.

lines.note: Extends the smoothing sense from creases in clothing to wrinkles in flesh. The provisional st spelling of estender is retained, without a global allograph normalization.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, permet. Dilatar o coração, & eſparecer.

lines.note: The figurative sense is to open or ease the heart and take recreation. Eſparecer is retained as printed rather than expanded to a modern-looking espairecer; Itẽ preserves the abbreviation mark.

runs.text: Lapas ſecas, & feitas em tiras compri-

lines.note: This separate noshi entry concerns dried shellfish cut into long strips. The later noshiawabi synonym identifies the awabi connection; the Portuguese itself uses Lapas, which remains unchanged.

runs.text: das que ſe guardão pera comer. No Ximo ſe

lines.note: Completes compridas and says the strips are kept for eating. Ximo is embedded in the regional Portuguese usage note, which continues with the local name below.
Completes the regional statement: in Ximo the item is called Noxiauabi. This is a Japanese term within an ongoing Portuguese explanation, not an independent headword here.
The independent noshiawabi entry refers the reader back to Noxi and asserts the same meaning. Only the cross-reference Noxi, not the ordinary headword, qualifies as an embedded typeface term.
Noshiba is illustrated by taka no noshiba, a hawk's extended wings. The Portuguese begins 'wings somewhat ...' and continues on f373; the isolated pouco below is its catchword, not another body row.
The italic catchword anticipates the first word of f373. The OCR's final l is the nearby vertical rule, not part of the word.
